    41	ICD-10 and DSM-5 do not provide clear diagnosing guidelines for DID, making it
    42	difficult to distinguish ‘genuine’ DID from imitated or false-positive cases. This study
    43	explores meaning which patients with false-positive or imitated DID attributed to their
    44	diagnosis. 85 people who reported elevated levels of dissociative symptoms in SDQ20 participated in
    45	clinical assessment using the Trauma and Dissociation Symptoms
    46	Interview, followed by a psychiatric interview. The recordings of six women, whose
    47	earlier DID diagnosis was disconfirmed, were transcribed and subjected to interpretative
    48	phenomenological analysis. Five main themes were identified: (1) endorsement and
    49	identification with the diagnosis. (2) The notion of dissociative parts justifies identity
    50	confusion and conflicting ego-states. (3) Gaining knowledge about DID affects the
    51	clinical presentation. (4) Fragmented personality becomes an important discussion
    52	topic with others. (5) Ruling out DID leads to disappointment or anger. To avoid
    53	misdiagnoses, clinicians should receive more systematic training in the assessment
    54	of dissociative disorders, enabling them to better understand subtle differences in the
    55	quality of symptoms and how dissociative and non-dissociative patients report them.
    56	This would lead to a better understanding of how patients with and without a dissociative
    57	disorder report core dissociative symptoms. Some guidelines for a differential diagnosis
    58	are provided.

    60	dissociation, differential
    61	diagnosis

    73	Dissociation, 2011), the prevalence of DID in the general population is estimated between 1 and
    74	3%. The review of global studies on DID in clinical settings by Sar (2011) shows the rate from

   145	for other forms of gratification (e.g., interest from others), while
   146	in many cases their motivation is not fully conscious. Getting
   147	a DID diagnosis can also provide structure for inner chaos and
   148	incomprehensible experiences, and be associated with hope and
   149	belief it is real. On the other hand, diagnostic errors often result

   177	the Study of Trauma and Dissociation, 2011; Dorahy et al.,

   181	(Leonard et al., 2005). Secondly, complex dissociative disorders
   182	are polysymptomatic, and specialists would rather diagnose these

   223	Unfortunately, ICD-10, ICD-11, and DSM-5 offer no specific
   224	guidelines on how to differentiate patients with personality

   227	distinguish between false-positive and false-negative DID. From

   232	Draijer, 1995; Draijer and Boon, 1999). Apart from observations

   305	MATERIALS AND METHODS
   306	This study was carried out in Poland in 2018 and

   399	Data Analysis
   400	Verbatim transcriptions were made of all video recordings, which
   401	were analyzed together with researchers’ notes using qualitative
   402	data-analysis software – NVivo11. Consecutive analytical steps
   403	recommended for IPA were employed in the study (Pietkiewicz

   405	the recording and carefully read the transcript several times.
   406	They individually made notes about body language, facial
   407	expressions, the content and language use, and wrote down
   408	their interpretative comments using the ‘annotation’ feature
   409	in NVivo10. Next, they categorized their notes into emergent
   410	themes by allocating descriptive labels (nodes). The team then
   411	compared and discussed their coding and interpretations. They
   412	analyzed connections between themes in each interview and
   413	between cases, and grouped themes according to conceptual
   414	similarities into main themes and sub-themes.

  1355	CONCLUSION
  1356	Clinicians need to understand the complexity of DID
  1357	symptoms and psychological mechanisms responsible

  1359	imitated post-traumatic conditions. There are several features
